# Boiling down: Construct validation/reliability, dimension reduction, factor analysis, and Psychometrics {#psychometrics}


## Constructs and construct validation and reliability

*Reliability vs validity:*

Reliability [wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reliability_(statistics)): "similar[ity] of results under similar conditions"

Validity of a tool [wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Validity_(statistics)): -- "the degree to which the tool measures what it claims to measure"

### Validity: general discussion 

> In psychometrics, validity has a particular application known as test validity: "the degree to which evidence and theory support the interpretations of test scores" ("as entailed by proposed uses of tests").


> Construct validity refers to the extent to which operationalizations of a construct (e.g., practical tests developed from a theory) measure a construct as defined by a theory. It subsumes all other types of validity.

There are a number of other measures and types of validity defined, some of which seem to involve subjective judgement, others of which are formalizable

\

### Reliability: general discussion 

Reliability of measurements and multicomponent measuring instruments:

- Inter-rater reliability
- Test-retest reliability
- Inter-method reliability
- Internal consistency reliability ("across items within a test.")

\
"Classical test theory"

> measurement errors are essentially random. ... they are not correlated with true scores or with errors on other tests.

> variance of obtained scores is simply the sum of the variance of true scores plus the variance of errors of measurement.

$$\sigma_{X}^{2}=\sigma_{T}^{2}+\sigma_{E}^{2}$$

> The reliability coefficient is defined as the ratio of true score variance to the total variance of test scores.

$$\rho_{XX'} = \sigma_T^2 / \sigma_X^2 = \sigma_T^2 / (\sigma_T^2 + \sigma_E^2)$$

<div class="marginnote">
Why is a larger reliability coefficient a good thing? I guess because it indicates that made the measurement error part as small as possible given the true score variance. But wouldn't it be better to choose a measure with a lower 'true score variance'?
</div>

:::: {.claude-explains}
**Claude explains: why higher reliability is better, and what it does to regressions** *(AI-written; not yet checked by David)*

::: {.fold}
True-score variance is the signal: real differences between people in the thing being measured. Error variance is noise. Reliability, $\sigma_T^2 / (\sigma_T^2 + \sigma_E^2)$, is the share of observed variation that is signal. A measure with little true-score variance cannot tell people apart, so lowering it would make the measure worse. The aim is low error variance relative to the real differences in the population studied. (The same instrument therefore has lower reliability in a more homogeneous sample.)

In econometric terms, reliability is the attenuation factor from classical measurement error:

- Noisy *regressor*: the OLS slope converges to $\beta \times$ reliability. With reliability 0.7, a true slope of 1 is estimated as 0.7. With other covariates correlated with the true regressor the attenuation is larger, because they absorb signal and leave the noise.
- Noisy *outcome*: the unstandardised coefficient is unbiased but less precise. Standardised effects (Cohen's $d$, correlations) shrink by $\sqrt{\text{reliability}}$, so $d = 0.5$ on the true score becomes $0.42$ on a measure with reliability 0.7.
- A correlation between two noisy measures is the true correlation times $\sqrt{r_X\, r_Y}$ (Spearman's attenuation formula).

All of this assumes the errors are unrelated to the true score and to each other. Two self-reports from the same survey often share error ('common methods bias', below), which can inflate a correlation.
:::
::::

**The basic problem** (?)

Paraphrasing...

> frequently ... in empirical social and behavioral research, we consider a measuring instrument consisting of a prespecified set of $p$ congeneric [related?] components denoted $X_1, ..., X_p$. ... 

> Let $T_1, ..., T_p$ and $E_1, ..., E_p$ be their corresponding true scores and error scores, respectively, with the latter assumed uncorrelated [to each other]

... Like 'measurement error' in Econometrics

> The scale components thus measure the same underlying latent dimension, designated $\xi$, with possibly different units and origins of measurement as well as error variances; that is,

$$X_i= T_i + E_i = \alpha_i + \beta_i \xi + E_i$$

Often used, of concern: the "composite (scale) score" $Z = X_1 + X_2 + \dots + X_p$  (e.g., Likert scale index)
